title: Bede (d. 735)
hook: the historian of England finished translating John as he died

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isidore of Seville, the bishop who gathered the learning of the world into one book. Your line was all knowledge. What was the new fact you learned, and who did you tell? Day seven hundred fifty-eight.

A monastery in the north of England, in spring. An old monk is very sick, and short of breath, and everyone around him can tell he's dying. He keeps working anyway. He's teaching, and singing psalms, and dictating to a young scribe, because there's a book he wants to finish. On the last day, the boy says there's still one sentence left to write. The old monk says, write it quickly. That monk, who wouldn't leave the sentence unfinished, is Bede.
screen: `A MONK IN THE NORTH OF ENGLAND.` → `TOO SICK, STILL WORKING.` → `ONE SENTENCE LEFT.`

segments.voice: Bede lived his life as a monk, praying the hours and writing. He wrote about the Bible, about time and the calendar, and above all a history of the Church among the English. That book is why he's remembered as a historian. He's careful in it. He often tells you where a story came from, who told it to him. Now, his death. We know about it because a monk named Cuthbert, one of his students, wrote it down in a letter. Cuthbert says that in his last days Bede was putting the Gospel of John into English, for the good of the Church, and also working on other passages. He kept dictating even as his breath failed. On the final day, the young scribe, Wilbert, said, there is still one sentence not written down. Bede told him to write it. A little later the boy said, now it is written. And Bede answered, you've spoken truly, it is finished. Cuthbert says he then asked to be held so he could face the place where he used to pray, and he died singing the Glory Be. A few days ago, Columba laid down his pen and left the next verse to the one who came after him. Bede did the opposite. And it is finished are the words John's Gospel gives Jesus on the cross. In the Douay-Rheims they read, "It is consummated." Some readers hear Bede's last words as a quiet echo of them. Catholics honor Bede as a saint and a Doctor of the Church, and call him the Venerable Bede. Today's carry is plain: finishing. Not finishing everything. Finishing the next sentence.
screen: `A HISTORIAN WHO NAMED HIS SOURCES.` · `JOHN'S GOSPEL INTO ENGLISH.` · `ONE SENTENCE NOT WRITTEN.` · then, large: `IT IS FINISHED.` · then: `FINISH THE NEXT SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: finish one sentence you started. Think of something left half done. An email sitting in drafts. A thank-you you meant to send. A page of a journal that stops mid-thought. A message to someone you love. Choose one. Don't fix the whole project. Just let yourself see the one sentence that would close it. Breathe slowly while you find the words. When the bell ends, go and write it down. If you pray, you can offer that small finished thing to God, the way Bede offered his. The bell holds the time.
Bede. A monk and historian of the English Church, who, by his student's account, kept dictating to the end and said, it is finished. Today's word.
Your line: finishing. Today, before you start anything new, finish one small thing you've left open, even one line of it. Day seven hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church keeps the feast of Saint Bede the Venerable and honors him as a Doctor of the Church; his history of the English Church is still read, and Cuthbert's letter about his death is often read alongside it.

original.note: Latin: it is finished — Jesus's word from the cross in the Latin Bible (John 19:30), which some readers hear in Bede's last words.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old English historian.
what it means: a monk who, by his student's account, kept working on John's Gospel in English until he died, and said, it is finished.
what a scholar hears: Cuthbert's letter on the death of Bede, which gives his last words in the Latin of the cross: consummatum est.

notes: Cuthbert's letter: Bede translating John into English up to 'but what are these among so many' (John 6:9), and extracts from Isidore; the boy Wilbert; 'one sentence not written'; 'it is finished' ('consummatum est'); dying on the floor of his cell singing the Gloria Patri. All paraphrased. Confirm details, especially the scribe's name and the exact Latin of Bede's reply.
'Some readers hear Bede's last words as an echo of John 19:30' is an interpretation; kept attributed.
Year of death (735) is the index title; not used in voice under the claims rule. 'In spring' (Ascension-tide) is from Cuthbert; confirm or cut.
'Spent his life in one monastic community': Bede says in HE 5.24 he lived at Wearmouth-Jarrow from childhood. Confirm phrasing (two houses, one community).
Bede naming sources: from his preface to the History. Confirm 'often'.
Venerable, saint, Doctor of the Church: confirm.

Editor: softened 'spent his life in one monastic community' (not in the cited texts); replaced the stock 'here's what's striking' with a short contrast to Columba's unfinished psalm (day 753), so the two deathbed-at-the-desk scenes read as a pair rather than a repeat.
Second editor: hook's doubled 'Today... Today' closing merged into one line; 'so ordinary people could hear it' (a motive Cuthbert's letter does not state) now 'for the good of the Church'.
Auditor: trapdoor no longer asserts Cuthbert's intent ('shapes his last words to echo the cross'); it now states only that the letter uses the Latin of John 19:30.
